title: Thirty scattered minutes
hook: Thirty free minutes in scattered gaps: will a 30-minute job fit?

knows: reading short labels and comparing simple counts
doesNotKnow: that a task that cannot be split needs one continuous gap as long as the task, and scattered gaps that add up to enough do not help

misconception: Thirty free minutes is thirty free minutes, even when it comes in pieces.
objective: Distinguish total free time from one continuous interval.

claims.text: An unsplittable task needs one continuous gap at least as long as it; 25 < 40, whatever the total.
claims.source: Recall item for this lesson: stipulated example data and the rule taught in the lesson (company/reviews/lifehacks-200/recall-patch-study.md + recall-patch-study.lines.txt). Applies to the example only; no empirical effect is claimed. Recall patch by learning-designer (session 2, 2026-10-14), applied by session 1. Pointer corrected by demo-builder 2026-10-14 (W-391a). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation on the stipulated values: the gaps 20, 15 and 25 total 60, the longest is 25, and 25 < 40. An unsplittable task needs one continuous interval at least as long as it (the lesson's rule, spec.principle; the schedule fixture likewise needs one 30-minute gap). The keyed option 'No; the longest gap is 25 minutes' is the only correct one; 'two largest gaps' (45) splits the task.

recall.question: Your afternoon has free gaps of 20, 15 and 25 minutes. Does a 40-minute task that cannot be split fit?
options: No; the longest gap is 25 minutes
Yes, using the two largest gaps
recall.why: An unsplittable task needs one continuous gap at least as long as it; 25 < 40, whatever the total.
